question_text: A streaming operator raises the monthly price of its video subscription and finds that the number of active subscriptions falls, with incomes and tastes unchanged. This outcome most directly illustrates:
options: The law of supply, where a higher price raises the quantity firms are willing to supply
The law of demand, where a higher price reduces the quantity demanded, other things equal
A leftward shift of the demand curve brought about by the change in the good's own price
A rise in demand elasticity that pushes the operator's total revenue upward as price rises
correct_answer: The law of demand, where a higher price reduces the quantity demanded, other things equal

question_text: Average household incomes in a region rise and, at every price, subscribers now buy more fixed broadband than before. For broadband treated as a normal good, this is best shown on a diagram as:
options: A rightward shift of the entire demand curve
A movement upward along the existing demand curve
A movement downward along the existing demand curve
A leftward shift of the entire supply curve
correct_answer: A rightward shift of the entire demand curve

question_text: Subscribers tend to buy a smartphone handset and a mobile data bundle together, so a fall in handset prices raises the quantity of data bundles bought. In demand analysis the two products are best classified as:
options: Substitute goods
Complementary goods
Inferior goods
Independent goods
correct_answer: Complementary goods

question_text: The market supply curve for a good is drawn holding other influences constant. Among the determinants of the quantity supplied, the variable placed at the centre of the basic supply relationship is the:
options: Price of the good itself
Level of consumer income in the market
Prices of goods that consumers regard as substitutes
Tastes and preferences of the buyers in the market
correct_answer: Price of the good itself

question_text: A component manufacturer offers more units for sale as the market price rises and fewer as it falls, with technology and input costs unchanged. This positive price-quantity relationship is captured by the:
options: Law of demand
Principle of diminishing marginal returns
Law of supply
Concept of consumer surplus
correct_answer: Law of supply

question_text: Engineers introduce a cheaper production technique that lowers the cost of making network routers. Holding the market price constant, standard analysis predicts that the supply curve for routers will:
options: Shift to the right, as producers offer more at each price
Shift to the left, as producers offer less at each price
Rotate until it becomes perfectly vertical at the old quantity
Stay fixed while buyers move downward along the demand curve
correct_answer: Shift to the right, as producers offer more at each price

question_text: Regulators observe that when the price of a basic voice service rises by 10 percent the quantity demanded falls by just 2 percent. The demand for this service is best described as:
options: Elastic, because quantity demanded responds sharply to the price change
Unit elastic, because quantity demanded falls in step with the price change
Inelastic, because quantity demanded responds little to the price change
Perfectly elastic, because quantity demanded collapses to zero after the change
correct_answer: Inelastic, because quantity demanded responds little to the price change

question_text: For a service with many close substitutes, a small price increase leads consumers to cut back their purchases sharply. The demand for such a service is best described as:
options: Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic
Elastic
correct_answer: Elastic

question_text: At the current market price of a good, the quantity that suppliers offer exceeds the quantity that buyers wish to purchase. Standard analysis predicts that the price will tend to:
options: Rise further above the equilibrium, widening the excess supply
Fall toward the equilibrium, clearing the excess supply
Stay fixed, since a surplus has no effect on the market price
Fall below the equilibrium and settle at a lasting shortage
correct_answer: Fall toward the equilibrium, clearing the excess supply

question_text: To keep a service affordable, a regulator caps its retail price below the market equilibrium and holds it there. Standard analysis predicts that this binding price ceiling will most likely produce:
options: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the capped price
A fresh equilibrium that settles exactly at the level of the capped price
A rise in supply large enough to remove the gap between demand and supply
A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price
correct_answer: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price

question_text: A government guarantees producers a minimum price set above the market equilibrium and commits to hold it there. The most likely consequence of this binding price floor is:
options: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the floor price
A swift movement of the market back to its original equilibrium price
A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the floor price
A fall in the quantity supplied to a level beneath the quantity demanded
correct_answer: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the floor price

question_text: In public finance, the phrase tax incidence is used specifically to describe:
options: How the economic burden of a tax ends up divided between buyers and sellers
The statutory rate that lawmakers write into the text of the tax legislation
The total revenue a government expects to raise from imposing the tax
The paperwork and collection costs a tax authority bears in administering the tax
correct_answer: How the economic burden of a tax ends up divided between buyers and sellers

question_text: A per-unit tax is levied on the buyers of a good rather than on its sellers. In the standard supply-and-demand model, the initial effect is represented as:
options: A rightward shift of the demand curve
A leftward shift of the supply curve
A rotation that makes the supply curve more elastic
A leftward (downward) shift of the demand curve
correct_answer: A leftward (downward) shift of the demand curve

question_text: An identical per-unit tax is placed on two goods. Good X has highly elastic demand while good Y has highly inelastic demand. Compared with buyers, sellers will tend to bear the larger share of the tax on:
options: Good X, where demand is elastic
Good Y, where demand is inelastic
Both goods in equal proportion, whatever the elasticities
Neither good, since the duty to remit the tax rests with buyers
correct_answer: Good X, where demand is elastic

question_text: An economy in which a central authority owns the major resources and directs what is produced, how, and for whom, is best described as a:
options: Traditional economy, coordinated by inherited custom
Market economy, coordinated mainly through prices
Mixed economy, blending markets with state action
Command economy, coordinated by central planning
correct_answer: Command economy, coordinated by central planning

question_text: An economy in which production methods and the allocation of goods follow inherited customs, with community elders having the final say, is best described as a:
options: Command economy
Market economy
Mixed economy
Traditional economy
correct_answer: Traditional economy

question_text: Supporters of the market economy argue that when buyers and sellers each pursue their own interest, competition and prices tend to guide resources toward valued uses. This coordinating tendency is often referred to as the:
options: Invisible hand of the market
Central plan of the state
Fixed rule of inherited custom
Visible hand of the regulator
correct_answer: Invisible hand of the market

question_text: A defining assumption of a perfectly competitive market is that:
options: A few large firms sell differentiated products and shade prices to match rivals
Many firms sell an essentially identical product, so no single firm sets the price
A single firm supplies the whole market and searches for its profit-maximising price
The state sets a common price that all the firms in the market then charge
correct_answer: Many firms sell an essentially identical product, so no single firm sets the price

question_text: Because a monopolist faces the whole market demand curve rather than a going market price, it is best described as a:
options: Price taker, which accepts the price set by the wider market
Quantity taker, which accepts an output level fixed by its rivals
Price maker, which chooses price and quantity along the demand curve
Cost taker, which accepts input prices dictated by the regulator
correct_answer: Price maker, which chooses price and quantity along the demand curve

question_text: An industry is described as a natural monopoly when, over the relevant range of output:
options: Several competing firms can serve the market more cheaply than one, owing to rivalry
The state licenses a single firm and bars new entrants from the market by statute
Firms coordinate their output so that the market behaves as though one firm supplied it, even while rivals remain active
One firm can serve the whole market at lower cost than several firms could, owing to economies of scale
correct_answer: One firm can serve the whole market at lower cost than several firms could, owing to economies of scale

question_text: Where a genuine natural monopoly supplies an essential service, a common regulatory response is to allow the single firm to remain but to:
options: Require several firms to duplicate the network regardless of the added cost
Step back from oversight and let the firm price the service as it sees fit
Regulate its prices and conduct so outcomes move closer to the competitive result
Take the firm and its rivals across the economy into full public ownership
correct_answer: Regulate its prices and conduct so outcomes move closer to the competitive result

question_text: A factory sells its output cheaply but discharges untreated waste that harms downstream communities whose losses it does not pay for. This gap between private and social cost is an example of a market failure known as a:
options: Positive externality
Public good
Price ceiling
Negative externality
correct_answer: Negative externality

question_text: On a supply-and-demand diagram, the area between the demand curve and the market price, up to the quantity traded, measures:
options: Consumer surplus, the gain buyers get above what they actually pay
Producer surplus, the gain sellers get above their marginal cost
Tax revenue, the amount the government raises from the market
Deadweight loss, the value of trades that fail to take place
correct_answer: Consumer surplus, the gain buyers get above what they actually pay

question_text: Compared with the competitive outcome, a profit-maximising monopoly restricts output and raises price. The value of the mutually beneficial trades that are lost as a result is referred to as the:
options: Producer surplus captured by the monopoly
Deadweight loss caused by the monopoly
Consumer surplus retained by the buyers
Tax incidence shared across the market
correct_answer: Deadweight loss caused by the monopoly

question_text: Because society's resources are limited while people's wants are not, every choice to use resources one way forgoes the next-best alternative. Economists call the value of that forgone alternative the:
options: Opportunity cost of the choice
Marginal revenue of the choice
Sunk cost of the choice
Fixed cost of the choice
correct_answer: Opportunity cost of the choice

question_text: In many countries before the 1980s, telephone services were run by a government post and telecommunications administration (a PTT). This arrangement meant the service was typically provided by:
options: A group of competing private carriers
A set of independent regional cooperatives
A state-owned monopoly
A foreign-owned equipment consortium
correct_answer: A state-owned monopoly

question_text: A frequently cited economic reason for the early telecom monopoly was that the high fixed cost of building a network, set against limited demand, made it hard for a second entrant to recover its outlay. This gave the industry the character of a:
options: Perfectly contestable market
Natural monopoly
Fully deregulated open market
Traditional subsistence economy
correct_answer: Natural monopoly

question_text: Beyond economics, a political reason governments kept telecommunications in state hands was that they:
options: Were barred by an international postal treaty from licensing a private telephone operator
Had no ministry with the technical means to oversee a basic national postal service
Regarded communications as strategically sensitive and wished to keep them under state control
Preferred to sell radio-spectrum rights straight to the highest private bidder of the day
correct_answer: Regarded communications as strategically sensitive and wished to keep them under state control

question_text: In the telecom sector, the term liberalization is best understood as:
options: The sale of a state operator's ownership to private shareholders
The setting of shared technical standards across the operators
The intervention of the state to reach particular market outcomes
The move from a monopoly market toward one open to competition
correct_answer: The move from a monopoly market toward one open to competition

question_text: When a regulator removes the incumbent's exclusive rights to provide certain services, the most direct effect of that step is to:
options: Move ownership of the incumbent's shares into private investors' hands
Let new entrants offer services that had been reserved for the incumbent
Grant the incumbent a longer, protected and exclusive market position
Fix a strict cap on the retail price of each of the incumbent's services
correct_answer: Let new entrants offer services that had been reserved for the incumbent

question_text: In the telecom sector, the term privatization refers specifically to:
options: Moving the ownership of an operator from the state to private hands
Opening a monopoly market to competition from new entrants
Placing universal-service duties on the licensed operators
Establishing a new and independent national regulatory body to supervise the sector
correct_answer: Moving the ownership of an operator from the state to private hands

question_text: A broad public offering of shares to many investors, rather than a sale to a single strategic buyer, has been the more common route to privatizing an incumbent in:
options: Developing countries with thin capital markets
Countries that never had an incumbent operator
Countries retaining a full state telephone monopoly
Highly industrialised countries
correct_answer: Highly industrialised countries

question_text: A country sells a majority stake in its incumbent fixed-line operator to private investors but continues to grant that operator exclusive rights over fixed services. This is best described as:
options: Liberalization of the market without privatization of the incumbent
Privatization of the incumbent without liberalization of the market
Both full liberalization and full privatization together
Neither privatization of the incumbent nor liberalization of the market
correct_answer: Privatization of the incumbent without liberalization of the market

question_text: In the context of the telecom sector, regulation is best defined as:
options: The full withdrawal of the government from the market's activity
The transfer of state-owned network assets into private ownership
Government intervention in a market to bring about particular desired outcomes
The routine self-policing of firms that operate without external oversight of their conduct
correct_answer: Government intervention in a market to bring about particular desired outcomes

question_text: Regulation is often said to take three basic forms. Setting common interconnection and equipment standards that let different operators' networks work together is an example of:
options: Public policy regulation
Competition regulation
Voluntary self-regulation
Technical standardization
correct_answer: Technical standardization

question_text: Requiring operators to carry emergency calls and to meet content rules judged to serve the public interest is an example of which basic form of regulation?
options: Public policy regulation
Technical standardization
Competition regulation
Co-regulation
correct_answer: Public policy regulation

question_text: The basic form of regulation aimed at establishing and preserving fair rivalry between firms, and fair dealing between firms and their customers, is:
options: Technical standardization
Public policy regulation
Competition regulation
Zero regulation
correct_answer: Competition regulation

question_text: Although telecom regulation can take several forms, the central focus of contemporary regulation of the telecommunications services industry is:
options: The harmonising of accounting standards across unrelated industries
The creation and maintenance of effective, competitive markets
The control of socially sensitive products such as alcohol
The removal of private ownership from the telecom sector
correct_answer: The creation and maintenance of effective, competitive markets

question_text: A widely recognised objective of telecom regulation is to protect the interests of consumers, for example by:
options: Securing a fixed profit margin for each of the licensed operators
Steering connectivity toward the most commercially attractive urban districts of the country
Addressing poor service quality and unfair terms that individual users struggle to resist
Holding back new operators that might enter and disturb the market
correct_answer: Addressing poor service quality and unfair terms that individual users struggle to resist

question_text: Where competitive markets are absent or have failed, a recognised objective is for the regulator to:
options: Guard against abuses of market power, such as excessive pricing by a dominant firm
Shelter the dominant firm from the entry of potential competitors
Pull back from oversight and let the market repair itself unaided
Set every operator's retail prices at one identical level right across the national market
correct_answer: Guard against abuses of market power, such as excessive pricing by a dominant firm

question_text: Which statement best captures the distinction between policy and law drawn in the course material?
options: Policy can compel or forbid conduct, whereas law merely offers broad guidance that binds no one
Policy and law mean the same thing, so the two terms can be swapped freely
Policy sets the long-term vision while law simply enforces it through the courts
Law can compel or forbid conduct, whereas policy sets a direction that guides action toward a goal
correct_answer: Law can compel or forbid conduct, whereas policy sets a direction that guides action toward a goal

question_text: Within the policy-to-practice chain, the role of regulation is chiefly to:
options: Turn the objectives set by policy into practical rules, decisions and day-to-day oversight
Define the broad, long-term national vision that takes shape well before policy itself is formed
Take the place of the underlying legislation and statutory authority
Review the personal finances of government ministers each year
correct_answer: Turn the objectives set by policy into practical rules, decisions and day-to-day oversight

question_text: A frequently noted problem in the pre-reform arrangement was that one government body often acted at the same time as policy maker, regulator and operator of the telephone service. The main concern with this was that it:
options: Left the day-to-day running of the telephone service without effective government supervision
Created conflicts of interest that made even-handed treatment of rivals difficult
Prevented the state from raising revenue through licence fees
Handed effective control of the sector to foreign carriers
correct_answer: Created conflicts of interest that made even-handed treatment of rivals difficult

question_text: The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) is best described as:
options: A private club funded by the world's largest mobile network operators
A regional trade bloc that negotiates import tariffs on telecom equipment on behalf of its members
A commercial standards firm owned and directed by major equipment vendors
A United Nations specialised agency dealing with information and communication technologies
correct_answer: A United Nations specialised agency dealing with information and communication technologies

question_text: Coordinating the international radio-frequency spectrum and satellite-orbit resources is the responsibility of which ITU sector?
options: ITU-T (Standardization)
ITU-D (Development)
ITU-P (Policy)
ITU-R (Radiocommunication)
correct_answer: ITU-R (Radiocommunication)

question_text: Developing the technical standards that let telecommunications networks and services interwork globally, apart from radio matters, is the responsibility of:
options: ITU-R (Radiocommunication)
ITU-D (Development)
ITU-T (Standardization)
ITU-S (Spectrum)
correct_answer: ITU-T (Standardization)

question_text: Helping to widen equitable, sustainable and affordable access to ICTs, especially in developing countries, is the principal role of:
options: ITU-D (Development)
ITU-R (Radiocommunication)
ITU-T (Standardization)
ITU-A (Access)
correct_answer: ITU-D (Development)

question_text: The World Trade Organization's Agreement on Basic Telecommunications (the BTA) is chiefly concerned with:
options: Assigning radio spectrum directly to individual operators in each member state
Setting out rules for competition and encouraging open investment in telecoms across countries
Fixing the maximum retail tariffs that operators may charge their subscribers
Granting individual operating licences directly to the carriers within each member state's market
correct_answer: Setting out rules for competition and encouraging open investment in telecoms across countries

question_text: One of the six basic principles of the WTO Reference Paper on Regulation is that interconnection with a major supplier should be:
options: Arranged privately between the largest carriers, on terms they keep confidential
Offered at whatever price the major supplier judges the market will bear
Provided on non-discriminatory terms, at cost-oriented rates and at reasonable request
Reserved for operators that the incumbent selects as suitable partners
correct_answer: Provided on non-discriminatory terms, at cost-oriented rates and at reasonable request

question_text: On the question of regulatory independence, the WTO Reference Paper and the course material indicate that a regulator should be independent of operators, while independence from government is:
options: Required by law, so the regulator must sit inside the sponsoring ministry
Required by law, so the regulator must be formally separate from government in all respects
Arranged so that the regulated operators jointly own and direct the regulator
Not strictly required, though a greater degree of it is generally regarded as desirable
correct_answer: Not strictly required, though a greater degree of it is generally regarded as desirable

question_text: Within the framework for regulation, the laws that governments pass to enable regulation characteristically:
options: Guarantee the incumbent a lasting and protected monopoly position
Establish regulatory bodies and grant them powers to act
Strip regulators of their duties to report and account for decisions
Set the retail price of each regulated service across the country
correct_answer: Establish regulatory bodies and grant them powers to act

question_text: Which option best lists the categories of law that bear specifically on the telecommunications services industry?
options: Maritime law, constitutional law and the criminal law of the state
General tax law, ordinary employment law and the intellectual-property law of everyday commercial dealings
Sector-specific telecom law, competition and fair-trading law, and other relevant law such as privacy
Banking law, insurance law and environmental law from other sectors
correct_answer: Sector-specific telecom law, competition and fair-trading law, and other relevant law such as privacy

question_text: Measures agreed by a regional body such as ECOWAS, or by the WTO, take legal effect within a member or signatory country once they are:
options: Transposed into national law in line with the treaty obligations
Posted on the regional body's official public website
Endorsed by a majority vote of the country's licensed operators
Agreed at the regional level, taking effect at that same moment
correct_answer: Transposed into national law in line with the treaty obligations

question_text: The framework notes that regulatory functions may be split between two or more bodies. A risk a country must manage when it does so is that:
options: A single national regulator will end up capturing the whole market for itself
Operators will find it much harder to obtain a licence from the divided bodies
A poorly designed split of functions can breed disputes and slow the making of decisions
Spectrum will end up handed to operators free of charge under the divided regulatory arrangement
correct_answer: A poorly designed split of functions can breed disputes and slow the making of decisions

question_text: Ranked from the least to the most intrusive, the recognised styles of regulation run:
options: Formal regulation, co-regulation, self-regulation, zero regulation
Zero regulation, self-regulation, co-regulation, formal regulation
Self-regulation, zero regulation, formal regulation, co-regulation
Co-regulation, formal regulation, zero regulation, self-regulation
correct_answer: Zero regulation, self-regulation, co-regulation, formal regulation

question_text: An industry said to operate under zero regulation is one in which:
options: A regulator supervises the firm's daily operations in fine detail
The firms jointly set binding rules under an industry watchdog
Market forces are left to work without outside intervention
A government ministry sets the prices at which firms must sell
correct_answer: Market forces are left to work without outside intervention

question_text: Self-regulation, in which the players in an industry set and police their own rules, tends to work best when:
options: The stakeholders share a strong convergence of interest
The players are locked in sharp commercial conflict with one another
One firm dominates the sector and mistrusts its smaller rivals
A regulator steps into the industry's routine operating decisions
correct_answer: The stakeholders share a strong convergence of interest

question_text: A commonly cited advantage of self-regulation is that:
options: It lifts the administrative cost of oversight from consumers and the industry alike
It keeps firms from behaving opportunistically toward their competitors
It removes the need for underlying legislation or a licensing regime
Firms usually understand their own business better than an outside regulator would
correct_answer: Firms usually understand their own business better than an outside regulator would

question_text: Co-regulation is best described as an arrangement in which:
options: The regulator works alongside industry players in a joint forum rather than ruling from outside
Firms run their own affairs with little external oversight of their conduct
A distant regulator dictates the firms' technical and pricing choices from outside the industry forum
A foreign body takes over the domestic regulatory authority for the sector
correct_answer: The regulator works alongside industry players in a joint forum rather than ruling from outside

question_text: Although it can be very effective, co-regulation is particularly exposed to:
options: Role ambiguity, where the players hold differing views of who will do what
A sudden and wholesale loss of the regulator's formal legal powers overnight
The capture of the regulator by organised consumer groups
A blanket legal ban on collaboration of this kind between firms
correct_answer: Role ambiguity, where the players hold differing views of who will do what

question_text: Regulation is described as intrusive when the regulator:
options: Sets out broad principles and leaves the methods to the firms themselves
Steps back from the market and lets market forces work unaided
Intervenes frequently and in fine detail in a company's day-to-day operations
Confines itself to issuing occasional, non-binding guidance
correct_answer: Intervenes frequently and in fine detail in a company's day-to-day operations

question_text: A reason intrusive regulation is generally viewed as undesirable is that:
options: It sharply lowers the total cost of supervising the whole industry closely
It assumes competition will deliver good outcomes without any oversight
It shifts responsibility for poor market outcomes from the regulator across onto the operating firms
The regulator drifts into acting as a proxy manager of the industry, weakening operators' freedom
correct_answer: The regulator drifts into acting as a proxy manager of the industry, weakening operators' freedom

question_text: Good practice suggests regulation should be pervasive rather than intrusive, meaning it should:
options: Shape operators' behaviour broadly while letting them run their own affairs within the rules
Prescribe the exact technical solution each operator is required to adopt
Have as little day-to-day effect on companies' operations as can be managed
Apply narrowly to just one dominant operator while leaving the other firms in the market untouched
correct_answer: Shape operators' behaviour broadly while letting them run their own affairs within the rules

question_text: Among the main instruments through which regulation is carried out are authorizations, rules, determinations, consents and:
options: Share buy-backs
Guidelines
Dividend payments
Corporate tax returns
correct_answer: Guidelines

question_text: A system of authorization may grant specific authorizations and general authorizations, which correspond respectively to:
options: Spectrum assignments and national numbering plans
Individual operator licences and class licences
Price-cap orders and interconnection determinations
Formal consents and published regulatory guidelines
correct_answer: Individual operator licences and class licences

question_text: Determinations are instruments of ongoing regulation whose function is essentially to:
options: Cancel an operator's licence at once, with no route of appeal against the decision
Overturn the underlying legislation suddenly and without prior notice
Offer advice that carries no legal weight and binds no one
Flesh out the rules, for example when price controls are reviewed periodically
correct_answer: Flesh out the rules, for example when price controls are reviewed periodically

question_text: Within the instruments of regulation, a consent is best understood as:
options: A negative determination that releases an operator from meeting a particular requirement
An order that places a fresh additional obligation on the particular operator concerned in the matter
An informal note that carries no legal standing in practice
A financial penalty imposed on an operator for breaching a licence term
correct_answer: A negative determination that releases an operator from meeting a particular requirement

question_text: Guidelines differ from rules and determinations in that guidelines:
options: Bind operators more tightly than the formal conditions attached to their own operating licences
Carry no legal force in themselves and are usually written in plain, accessible language
Are issued by the courts following a successful appeal by an operator
Cancel a licence at the very moment the operator is found to breach them
correct_answer: Carry no legal force in themselves and are usually written in plain, accessible language

question_text: A key reason regulators consult widely before finalising their instruments is that consultation:
options: Transfers the formal power of decision straight to the parties that are being consulted
Relieves the regulator of its duty to give reasons for a decision
Gives industry ownership of, and early sight of, decisions and improves their quality
Discourages the consulted parties from appealing the final outcome
correct_answer: Gives industry ownership of, and early sight of, decisions and improves their quality

question_text: An appeal against a regulator's action may be brought on the grounds of law (illegality), procedure (misadministration) or:
options: Profitability (loss of revenue)
Logic (irrationality)
Popularity (public disapproval)
Timing (administrative delay)
correct_answer: Logic (irrationality)

question_text: Which of the following is a recognised enforcement power a regulator may use against an operator that breaks the rules?
options: Seizing ownership of a competitor's shareholding
Personally setting the salaries paid to each of the operator's own board of directors
Barring the operator's customers from switching providers
Imposing fines, issuing compliance orders, or in serious cases revoking the licence
correct_answer: Imposing fines, issuing compliance orders, or in serious cases revoking the licence

question_text: On the funding of national regulatory authorities, the typical arrangement is that:
options: Operators are barred by law from contributing to the regulator's budget
Government carries the primary responsibility but usually recovers the cost from industry through fees
The regulator supports itself mainly on the fines it collects from ordinary telecom subscribers each year
The budget comes chiefly from foreign donor agencies and aid grants
correct_answer: Government carries the primary responsibility but usually recovers the cost from industry through fees

question_text: The idea of regulatory hazard captures the concern that:
options: Regulators face genuine physical danger to themselves when they inspect live network sites in the field
Regulation strips most of the commercial risk out of the telecom market
Regulatory power, if used unwisely, can distort markets and damage the industry it oversees
Operators face no consequences for repeatedly breaching the rules
correct_answer: Regulatory power, if used unwisely, can distort markets and damage the industry it oversees

question_text: Regulatory capture is said to occur when:
options: The regulator becomes gridlocked and stops issuing decisions for a long spell
The regulator comes to identify with the industry it oversees and serves that industry's interests
Individual operators are taken over and then run directly by the regulator acting as their outright owner
Consumers step in and take charge of the regulator's day-to-day running
correct_answer: The regulator comes to identify with the industry it oversees and serves that industry's interests

question_text: The information asymmetry that regulators face arises mainly because:
options: Regulators are forbidden by statute from gathering the operators' detailed cost and operating data
Consumers deliberately hide their true preferences from the regulator
Operators are obliged by statute to withhold their internal financial records
The firms being regulated usually know far more about their business than the regulator does
correct_answer: The firms being regulated usually know far more about their business than the regulator does

question_text: Regulators grant licences to companies mainly in order to authorise them to:
options: Operate telecommunications networks and provide telecommunications services
Manufacture and export telecommunications equipment to buyers in other markets
Set the country's monetary and fiscal policy for the wider economy
Audit the financial accounts of competing operators each year
correct_answer: Operate telecommunications networks and provide telecommunications services

question_text: Beyond granting permission to operate, a telecommunications licence characteristically sets out:
options: The exact retail prices that every other operator in the country must charge
The internal staffing structure and the full organisation chart of the sector's own regulatory authority
The facilities a company may deploy, the services it may offer, and how it deals with other operators
The personal income-tax liabilities of the company's individual directors
correct_answer: The facilities a company may deploy, the services it may offer, and how it deals with other operators

question_text: For major licences that also govern access to scarce resources such as spectrum and numbers, operators are commonly required to pay:
options: A fixed share of yearly profits handed to the competing operators
An upfront fee when the licence is awarded, followed by annual payments
No payment, since major licences are usually granted free of charge
A one-off refundable deposit returned in full when the licence expires
correct_answer: An upfront fee when the licence is awarded, followed by annual payments

question_text: Historically, telecom licences were issued separately for different sub-markets such as fixed, mobile or paging services. The defining feature of that approach was that the licences:
options: Were designed to be broadly technology- and service-neutral
Applied identical terms across each and every market segment
Were rarely tied to a specific technology or class of service
Drew distinctions between particular technologies and services
correct_answer: Drew distinctions between particular technologies and services

question_text: The convergence of technologies, which lets different platforms deliver overlapping services, has led some regulators to shift toward:
options: Technology- and service-neutral licensing
Tighter technology-specific licensing for each platform
The withdrawal of the licensing regime altogether
Long, protected exclusive licences for the incumbents
correct_answer: Technology- and service-neutral licensing

question_text: A technology-neutral licence to provide a telephone service is one that:
options: Obliges the operator to use one particular government-specified fixed access technology
Prevents the operator from offering any voice service of its own
Leaves the operator free to choose between a fixed network and a wireless technology
Requires the operator to buy from a single approved equipment vendor
correct_answer: Leaves the operator free to choose between a fixed network and a wireless technology

question_text: The two main categories of licence awarded to telecom companies are:
options: Individual operator licences and class licences (general authorizations)
Spectrum-only licences and separate telephone-numbering licences
Import licences and export licences for telecom equipment
Short-term provisional licences and longer-term probationary trial licences
correct_answer: Individual operator licences and class licences (general authorizations)

question_text: Individual operator licences are used chiefly where:
options: The market segment has ample room for many further new entrants
The segment involves no scarce technical resources of any kind
The particular market segment has ample room for many further new entrants to join and compete on equal terms
Licences are limited in number, dominance is likely, or scarce resources such as spectrum must be assigned
correct_answer: Licences are limited in number, dominance is likely, or scarce resources such as spectrum must be assigned

question_text: Class licences (general authorizations) are characterised by the fact that they:
options: Are tailored individually to a single, specifically named operator within the market segment concerned
Apply the same terms of operation to all businesses in a segment, such as internet service providers
Are reserved for the use of the former state incumbent operator
Apply in the cases where radio spectrum has to be assigned
correct_answer: Apply the same terms of operation to all businesses in a segment, such as internet service providers

question_text: A current trend favours replacing individual operator licences with general authorizations where practical, because doing so:
options: Maximises the one-off upfront revenue that the state collects from each licensed operator at the award stage
Simplifies regulation, supports a level playing field, and adapts more readily to market change
Locks in the incumbent's protected position for a long period
Removes the need for an independent regulator in the sector
correct_answer: Simplifies regulation, supports a level playing field, and adapts more readily to market change

question_text: One licensing objective treats basic telecommunications as an essential public service. This is used to justify:
options: Lifting regulatory oversight the moment the market is privatised
Reserving service provision for a single state-owned monopoly for the long term
Keeping some controls so that services are provided in the public interest
Letting operators serve just the most profitable customers
correct_answer: Keeping some controls so that services are provided in the public interest

question_text: Network roll-out targets and coverage obligations are often written into licences chiefly to advance which licensing objective?
options: The raising of one-off government revenue from spectrum auctions
The shielding of the incumbent operator from new competition
The harmonising of company accounting and reporting practices
The expansion of networks and services, and universal service
correct_answer: The expansion of networks and services, and universal service

question_text: When a state-owned incumbent is privatized, a licence remains necessary because it:
options: Transfers full legal ownership and operational control of the regulator across to the investor
Assures the investor of lasting freedom from future regulation
Lifts the operator's duty to serve less profitable customers
Sets out what the investor is buying and what the government expects the operator to do
correct_answer: Sets out what the investor is buying and what the government expects the operator to do

question_text: Licensing can be used to shape the structure of a market most directly by:
options: Fixing the wholesale price of each input used on the network
Deciding how many operators are licensed to provide a given service
Setting the wages that an operator pays its own employees
Choosing the equipment vendors that operators are required to use
correct_answer: Deciding how many operators are licensed to provide a given service

question_text: Licence conditions intended to create a level playing field and to curb an incumbent's abuse of dominance are usually referred to as:
options: Universal-service obligations for underserved regions
Spectrum-refarming and reallocation provisions
Tariff-rebalancing and price-adjustment schedules
Anti-competitive safeguards, or fair-trading conditions
correct_answer: Anti-competitive safeguards, or fair-trading conditions

question_text: As a licensing objective, finite resources such as radio spectrum, numbers and rights of way should be allocated:
options: In full to whichever operator has the longest trading history
On a first-come basis with little regard to how efficiently they are used
Between operators fairly, efficiently and in the public interest
To the operators that happen to be owned by the state
correct_answer: Between operators fairly, efficiently and in the public interest

question_text: Licensing generates government revenue in two characteristic ways:
options: Seizure of operator profits and the taking of their network assets by the state
Personal income taxes levied directly on the regulator's own staff
Yearly donations collected from international agencies and donors
One-off revenue from auctions and continuing revenue from annual licence fees
correct_answer: One-off revenue from auctions and continuing revenue from annual licence fees

question_text: Consumer-protection conditions in telecom licences commonly deal with matters such as:
options: Billing accuracy, complaint-handling arrangements and required services such as emergency calls
The internal shareholding structure of the operator's parent holding company and its subsidiaries
The personal credit ratings of the operator's individual directors
The choice of external auditors used by the regulator itself
correct_answer: Billing accuracy, complaint-handling arrangements and required services such as emergency calls

question_text: By setting out clearly the rights and duties of the operator and the regulator, a licence advances the objective of:
options: Regulatory certainty, which builds confidence and helps attract investment
Spectrum refarming carried out across the competing operators
The removal of the regulator's remaining discretion over its own day-to-day decisions
An exactly equal share of the national market for each operator
correct_answer: Regulatory certainty, which builds confidence and helps attract investment

question_text: The international allocation of radio spectrum, designed to maximise its use while limiting cross-border interference, is coordinated by the:
options: World Trade Organization (WTO)
Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
Association of the operators within each country
correct_answer: International Telecommunication Union (ITU)

question_text: Although telephone numbers are in principle plentiful, they are treated as a scarce resource partly because:
options: There is a small and strictly fixed stock of usable telephone-number digits in existence around the world
People can recall only a limited string of digits, and numbers must be issued in meaningful blocks
Each telephone number needs its own dedicated radio frequency to work
A given number can be assigned to just one country across the world
correct_answer: People can recall only a limited string of digits, and numbers must be issued in meaningful blocks

question_text: Number portability is a mechanism by which:
options: The subscriber effectively owns the number and can carry it when switching providers
The operator keeps lasting ownership of the telephone numbers that it issues to its subscribers
Numbers are auctioned off periodically to whichever operator bids the most
Subscribers take a new number each time they move to a different provider
correct_answer: The subscriber effectively owns the number and can carry it when switching providers

question_text: A regulator may auction spectrum to the highest bidder or assign it at a low administered price. Assigning spectrum at a low price is typically intended to:
options: Maximise the one-off revenue the government collects
Set aside the band for the use of a single operator
Lower prices for users or encourage the rollout of new services
Remove the practical need to manage radio interference between competing users
correct_answer: Lower prices for users or encourage the rollout of new services

question_text: A primary reason spectrum is assigned through instruments such as licences, rather than used freely, is to:
options: Increase the stock of digits available for telephone numbers nationally
Let each operator broadcast on whichever radio frequency it happens to prefer at the time
Ensure it is distributed sensibly and that users do not interfere with one another
Remove the need for any coordination of frequencies across borders
correct_answer: Ensure it is distributed sensibly and that users do not interfere with one another

question_text: The core principle of interconnection is that:
options: Each operator should deliberately keep its own subscribers walled off from the networks of rivals
Everyone should be able to communicate with everyone else, whichever network they belong to
Operators of a broadly similar size are the ones required to interconnect
Interconnection is required between the largest international carriers
correct_answer: Everyone should be able to communicate with everyone else, whichever network they belong to
